items.title: India's CAD may touch 1.2% of GDP in FY27 as oil, gold demand pose risks: UBI
items.summary: India's current account deficit is projected to reach 1.2% of GDP in FY27, driven by oil prices, according to a report by Union Bank of India. The report emphasizes that high crude oil prices and gold demand could impact the external balance. Merchandise trade deficit widened to a significant USD 39.88 billion in October. Additionally, imports surged while services trade surplus remained nearly flat during the same period.

events.article_text:
India's current account deficit is projected to reach 1.2% of GDP in FY27, driven by oil prices, according to a report by Union Bank of India. The report emphasizes that high crude oil prices and gold demand could impact the external balance. Merchandise trade deficit widened to a significant USD 39.88 billion in October. Additionally, imports surged while services trade surplus remained nearly flat during the same period.

analysis.tldr: India's foreign trade account could face some pressure down the road, meaning the rupee could weaken and make imported items like petrol and electronics costlier.
the_story: Union Bank of India projected that India's current account deficit (the gap between total money going out of the country and coming in) may touch 1.2% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP, the total value of all goods and services produced) in the financial year 2027.
This projected widen is driven mainly by high crude oil prices and continued gold demand.
India's merchandise trade deficit (the gap specifically between physical goods bought from and sold to other countries) widened to a significant USD 39.88 billion in October.
During the same October period, imports surged while the services trade surplus (net earnings from selling intangible services like IT abroad) remained nearly flat.
analysis.what_happened: Union Bank of India released a report warning that India's trade gap is growing. This is being caused by a surge in physical imports, a massive trade deficit hitting USD 39.88 billion in October, and a steady appetite for foreign oil and gold while service exports failed to grow enough to balance it out.
analysis.analogy: It is like a household whose monthly grocery and shopping bills (imports) suddenly grow much larger than their salary from the office (exports), forcing them to draw down their savings to pay the difference.
why_it_matters_india: India buys most of its crude oil and gold from foreign countries by paying in US dollars.
When imports surge and the trade deficit widens, India needs significantly more foreign currency than it earns.
This higher demand for dollars puts downward pressure on the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
A weaker rupee automatically makes all essential imports like crude oil more expensive, which can eventually spark domestic inflation (rising prices of everyday goods).

impacts.rationale: A wider trade deficit means India demands more foreign currency to pay for imports, which can cause the rupee to weaken — making imported goods costlier for regular people.
Strong and persistent domestic gold demand mentioned in the report, combined with a weaker rupee, generally pushes up the local cost of buying gold.
High crude oil prices driven by import demand, coupled with a potentially weaker rupee, can eventually feed into higher fuel prices at Indian petrol pumps.

watch_next: Monthly updates on India's merchandise trade deficit numbers
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and a short excerpt were available, meaning the broader long-term economic forecasts rely on limited context from the Union Bank of India report.

analysis.tldr: Cheaper crude oil lowers inflation worries, meaning the government can borrow money more cheaply and your future loans could become more affordable.
the_story: Indian government bonds saw an increase in value during early trading.
Crude oil prices dropped significantly, which is expected to ease inflation (rising prices) and reduce fears of aggressive rate hikes (central banks raising borrowing costs).
The benchmark 6.94% 2036 bond yield (the interest rate the government pays to borrow) fell to 7.2813%.
Lower oil prices also support the local rupee (India's currency) and the current account deficit (the gap between what India buys from abroad and sells).
analysis.what_happened: Indian government bonds rose because crude oil prices dropped significantly in early trading. When oil gets cheaper, it relieves pressure on India's inflation and trade balance, which calms market fears that interest rates might be hiked aggressively. This caused the return on long-term government bonds to fall.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family budget suddenly getting breathing room because your monthly petrol bill drops, meaning you have more spare cash and do not need to stress about borrowing money at higher interest rates.
why_it_matters_india: Crude oil prices drop in global markets
Fears of high inflation and aggressive interest rate hikes fade away
Government bond yields fall because investors demand lower returns when inflation is calm
Overall borrowing costs for the economy stabilize, making future loans potentially cheaper for everyone

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Lower yields mean the government and wider economy can borrow money more cheaply, which is generally good for borrowers.
Cheaper oil reduces the amount of dollars India needs to spend on imports, helping the local currency stay stable or strengthen.
Falling global crude prices relieve cost pressures on fuel, which can ultimately benefit household budgets if passed on.

analysis.caveats: If global oil prices suddenly spike back up due to sudden supply shocks, bond gains could reverse quickly.

events.headline: Libya Has Africa's Biggest Oil Reserves, but Western Majors Aren't Biting

items.title: Libya Has Africa's Biggest Oil Reserves, but Western Majors Aren't Biting
items.summary: In the immediate aftermath of Russia’s 24 February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the pressure was on the West to quickly find new sources of oil and gas to compensate for those from Russia that would be lost through initial supply-chain disturbances and then because of sanctions. events.article_text:
Japan Proposes an 'Asian IEA' to Protect Oil Supplies

Simon Watkins is a former senior FX trader and salesman, financial journalist, and best-selling author. He was Head of Forex Institutional Sales and Trading for…

In the immediate aftermath of Russia’s 24 February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the pressure was on the West to quickly find new sources of oil and gas to compensate for those from Russia that would be lost through initial supply-chain disturbances and then because of sanctions. The net was cast wide, as several major possibilities in the world’s main aggregate source of hydrocarbons had already moved more firmly in the run-up to the invasion into China’s and Russia’s sphere of influence. This included Saudi Arabia and the UAE, both of whose de facto leaders refused even to take a telephone call from then-President Joe Biden to talk about helping to reduce spiralling oil and gas prices by producing more, as analysed in full in my latest book on the new global oil market order. Qatar was a notable early exception in the region, becoming such a key supplier of liquefied natural gas to European allies of the U.S. that it was designated a ‘Major Non-NATO Ally’, as was Egypt, which had a multilayered strategic importance to the West, as it did to the East, as also detailed in the book. Perhaps the most unexpected country to which Washington and its allies directed their attention was Libya, but investment plans were made and money flowed in, helping to push its oil production up to a 13-year high of 1.4-1.5 million barrels per day (bpd). However, recent indications suggest that this Western rush may already be fading -- raising serious questions over what comes next for Libya’s oil sector.

A key signal for concern was the distinctly underwhelming Western response to Libya’s February 2026 licensing awards -- the first since 2007 and specifically touted by Tripoli as likely to mark the beginning of a new upsurge of investment across the country’s oil and gas sector. As at the close of the licensing round, only five out of 22 blocks had been awarded, comprising Offshore Block 22 (Sirte Basin) going to Spain’s Repsol, Turkey’s TPAO, and Hungary’s MOL; Offshore Area 01 (Sirte/Cyrenaica) going to Italy’s Eni and QatarEnergy; Onshore Contract Area 106 (Sirte Basin) going to the U.S.’s Chevron; Onshore C3 (Sirte Basin) also going to Repsol and TPAO; and, Onshore M1 (Murzuq Basin) going to Nigeria’s Aiteo Group. It was triply disappointing because not only was the final number so small, but also because there had been 37 companies that pre-qualified, but many of them ultimately declined even to submit a final bid. Additionally, despite Libya’s state-owned National Oil Corporation (NOC) pitching the licensing round as also marking an historic return of Western supermajors, more than 75 percent of the blocks offered remained unsold, and heavyweights like Shell, TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil, and BP either sat out the round entirely or declined to submit binding bids.

It is true that last week saw the NOC discuss exploration plans for the second quarter of 2027 with a consortium including Repsol, TPAO and MOL, but this only concerns Offshore Block 22 in the Sirte Basin, with first oil in such an ultra-deepwater site typically likely to take six to 10 years to emerge. Any jump in Libya’s oil production over the short- to medium-term towards the NOC’s stated 2.1 million bpd longer-term target would instead have to come from the rehabilitation of mature onshore fields, including Sharara, El Feel, Waha, and brownfield areas in the Sirte Basin. However, in both the latest licensing round and in separate negotiations, major Western oil firms are once again looking increasingly reticent to commit to long-term capital investment in Libya. The already entrenched European majors -- Eni (which dominates Libyan gas exports to Italy) and Repsol (heavily invested in Sharara) -- appeared to use the latest licensing round simply to hedge their existing exposure in Libya by taking deepwater offshore blocks that are physically insulated from onshore pipeline militias. Meanwhile, Chevron’s single onshore block looks more like a placeholder for potential future activities rather than a signal of major planned investment.

In theory, it looks a compelling potential opportunity, with the country holding around 48 billion barrels of proved crude reserves -- the largest in Africa. Before Muammar Gaddafi was removed from the leadership in 2011, Libya had no difficulty sustaining output of roughly 1.65 million bpd of high-quality light, sweet crude. The flagship grades, Es Sider and Sharara, were especially prized in the Mediterranean and Northwest Europe for their strong gasoline and middle-distillate yields. Production had also been on a steady upward path, rising from about 1.4 million bpd in 2000, even if still far below the more than 3 million bpd achieved in the late 1960s. Crucially, though, the NOC had already laid out plans before 2011 to deploy enhanced oil recovery (EOR) techniques across maturing fields. Its estimate that EOR could add around 775,000 bpd of capacity looked entirely credible, and Western interest in new upstream developments showed no sign of fading at the time.

However, in practice, the key reason for the reticence of Western oil firms to become more deeply involved in the country remains the extraordinarily precarious security situation there. This all dates back to same basic problem of how the oil revenues in the country should be disbursed that were highlighted during the landmark peace agreement negotiated on 18 September 2020 to end the previous mammoth blockade of oil. At the time, Commander of the rebel Libyan National Army (LNA), General Khalifa Haftar, made it clear to the opposing side with which the deal had been struck -- Tripoli’s UN-recognised Government of National Accord (GNA) -- that the agreement would be an interim arrangement only, while a solution was worked out on oil

analysis.tldr: Weak foreign interest in Libya's oil fields leaves global supply tight, keeping crude oil prices elevated which makes imported energy costlier for India.
the_story: Libya's February 2026 licensing awards—its first since 2007—saw a disappointing response, with only 5 out of 22 oil and gas blocks awarded despite 37 companies pre-qualifying.
Major global energy heavyweights like Shell, TotalEnergies, ExxonMobil, and BP sat out the round entirely or chose not to submit binding bids.

Existing European players like Spain's Repsol, Italy's Eni, and Turkey's TPAO took blocks mainly to protect their current investments, while U.S. firm Chevron took a single onshore block as a small placeholder.
The primary reason Western oil firms hesitate to invest in Libya is the extremely precarious security situation and ongoing disputes over how oil revenues are distributed among local factions.
analysis.what_happened: Libya tried to auction off new oil exploration rights to attract global companies and boost its production. However, most big Western energy firms refused to participate due to severe local security risks and political fighting, meaning Libya's massive oil reserves will stay mostly locked away.
analysis.analogy: It is like a shopkeeper offering a huge discount on a massive warehouse full of goods, but shop owners refuse to buy because the neighborhood is too dangerous to visit.
why_it_matters_india: Libya fails to expand its oil production significantly because foreign companies refuse to invest.
Global oil supply stays lower than it could have been, keeping international crude prices higher.
India imports over 80% of its crude oil needs, making the country heavily dependent on global oil prices.
Higher oil import costs increase domestic fuel prices and push up inflation (the rate at which prices rise), putting pressure on the Indian rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).

impacts.rationale: Lack of new oil production from Libya keeps global supply restricted, which pushes oil prices higher — bad for energy-importing nations like India.
Costlier imported oil means India needs to spend more dollars, weakening the rupee — bad for everyday citizens as imported goods get expensive.
Higher crude prices eventually raise transportation and manufacturing costs across the economy, driving up everyday consumer prices — bad for household budgets.
Pricier global crude feeds into higher fuel pump prices over time — bad for vehicle owners and commuters.

watch_next: Future oil production output reports from Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC)
Global crude oil inventory and price movements
analysis.caveats: If other major oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia or the U.S. pump more oil to cover the gap, Libya's missing production might not affect global prices much.

events.headline: Why India's rupee defence needs a rethink

items.title: Why India's rupee defence needs a rethink
items.summary: Despite interventions, FCNR(B) deposits and new regulations, pressure on the rupee persists. India should look beyond crisis tools and focus on a competitive exchange rate, calibrated interest rates and stronger export capacity.

events.article_text:
India’s forex reserves declined from its historic peak of $785.71 billion on 4 September 2026 to $719.75 billion on 23 October 2026, a wipeout of $66 billion in 49 days.

Around 50% of the forex inflows accumulated through the special Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank FCNR(B) deposit scheme has already been used to defend the rupee through reported forex market interventions.

In the last six months, the rupee has faced sustained pressure. From interventions in spot and forward markets to FCNR-B and foreign exchange risk reserve (FERR), a series of measures have been tried. Their effectiveness remains uncertain. It is time to reassess whether the current approach can address the underlying pressures on the currency.

In 1991, India initiated major economic and external-sector reforms, under the shadow of BOP crises. What appeared then as decisions under duress turned out to be beneficial: as Indian markets opened to the world, competitiveness in key export areas emerged. Indian rupee remained loosely tethered to the dollar thereafter.

However, two concerns remained: the sustained depreciation of the rupee (the rupee rising from ₹35.43 in 1996 to ₹87.17 against the dollar in 2025, an increase of about 146%) punctuated by periodic crises, notably in 2013 and, more recently, from 2021 onwards; and the failure of exports to grow sufficiently despite this depreciation.

In 2013, the rupee had one of its worst crises following the taper tantrum, showing clearly that the Fed’s actions (and inactions even) may sometimes have a greater impact than domestic conditions. To support the rupee, the RBI came up with a series of measures that have since formed a sort of rulebook: measures to control imports, attract capital inflows (the occasional FCNR-B), spot- and forward-market interventions and finally communication to market participants.

First, spot-market interventions in the forex market have repercussions on the domestic side: a sale of USD dries up liquidity, requiring an offsetting liquidity operation. FX swaps, as a tool for forward-market intervention, therefore became very common from 2013 onwards.

When domestic liquidity dries up following a forex sale, the central bank does a buy-sell swap: buy-dollar leg will initially infuse rupee liquidity (spot), while the sale of dollars will take place later (forward), anywhere between three months and three years down the line. Effectively, this is a postponement of the dollar liabilities into the future. Figure 1 shows how RBI’s short positions ballooned in recent past.

Second, effectiveness of import controls and export promotion is constrained by both India's dependence on oil, and the lack of alternative energy sources and the fact that a weaker rupee alone cannot guarantee export competitiveness.

Third, FCNR(B)-like schemes, while attractive, are essentially a form of borrowing from NRIs abroad. The deposits have to be repaid in the future, making it a liability. Moreover, the increase in reserves from such schemes can be wiped away in a matter of days if continued interventions are carried out to support the currency in the face of increased speculation (Figure 2).

Fourth, the RBI has recently introduced a series of measures, from regulations on bank’s net open positions to FERR. Under FERR, a 20% cash reserve requirement on the rupee equivalent of the notional amount of each transaction exceeding $2 million is mandated: for purchase of foreign currency to hedge current-account transactions.

However, these are more stopgap measures. The latest measure worryingly may further discourage hedging in a market where firms reluctantly hedge.

Crucially, most emerging markets, including India, ‘follow’ the US Federal Reserve. Interest rates in a growing economy need not necessarily determine either the profitability of businesses or their ability to undertake capital expenditure. If this were so, the prolonged period of low interest rates would have seen substantial capital expenditure.

A moderately higher interest rate may usher greater saving and support exports. Notably, India’s high growth trajectory during 2002-2008 also coincides with a high-interest-rate regime. Beyond inflation management, calibrated interest-rate measures influencing exchange rates can provide cushion against supply-side shocks.

Finally, central bank communication is a tricky tool, embedded, as it is, with time consistency problems. RBI has reiterated, in recent few years, that India has a ‘market-determined’ exchange rate. However, there are continued reports of interventions in the forex market. Does it lead to a disconnect between words, policies, and actions? A single unguarded statement like 100 being ‘just a number’ from anyone related to policymaking may reduce the credibility of the policy mechanism.

Going forward, controlling inflation on the domestic side and increasing exports by allowing the rupee to remain as competitive as possible may help. India has considerable advantages in sectors such as IT, engineering goods, and gems and jewellery. A key factor that could contribute to the success of exports is the growth of the small and micro industries. Once small businesses scale and access global markets, it would not be difficult to build an export-oriented economy. This would also require a highly competitive rupee for smaller players.

Smita Roy Trivedi is associate professor, National Institute of Bank Management (NIBM); Abhiman Das is ICICI Bank chair professor, Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad (IIMA). Views are strictly personal.

analysis.tldr: Heavy spending to protect the rupee has drained billions from India's safety reserves, sparking a debate on whether the central bank should let the currency find its natural level instead.
the_story: India's forex reserves (foreign currency and gold savings held by the central bank) dropped by $66 billion in just 49 days, falling from $785.71 billion on 4 September 2026 to $719.75 billion on 23 October 2026.
Around 50% of the money collected through a special NRI (Non-Resident Indian) deposit scheme called FCNR-B has already been spent to defend the rupee through market interventions.
The rupee has depreciated significantly over the decades, rising from ₹35.43 per dollar in 1996 to ₹87.17 in 2025, while exports have failed to grow enough despite this slide.

The RBI (Reserve Bank of India, the country's central banking institution) uses various tools to defend the currency, including spot-market dollar sales, forward-market swaps, import controls, and strict bank regulations like FERR (Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve, a 20% cash lock requirement on large hedging transactions).

The authors argue that these stopgap measures are costly liabilities and suggest that letting the rupee adjust naturally while focusing on domestic inflation and small business exports might be a better strategy.
analysis.what_happened: India's central bank has been burning through its foreign exchange reserves at an alarming speed—losing $66 billion in under two months—to prevent the rupee from falling too fast against the US dollar. Because past tools like borrowing from NRIs and complex currency swaps are only temporary fixes that create future financial liabilities, experts are warning that this heavy defense strategy needs a total rethink.
analysis.analogy: It is like draining your family's entire emergency medical savings account just to pay for day-to-day household expenses, hoping things will magically get cheaper tomorrow, instead of adjusting your budget.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI spends its dollar reserves to buy rupees and slow down the currency's fall.
Spending these reserves drains the country's financial safety cushion down from its peak of $785.71 billion.
If the RBI stops heavily defending the currency, the rupee may weaken faster, making imported goods like crude oil and electronics more expensive for everyday consumers.
A weaker rupee could eventually make Indian exports more competitive, helping sectors like IT, engineering goods, and gems and jewellery if small businesses are able to scale up.

impacts.rationale: If the central bank rethinks its heavy defense and lets the market dictate rates, the rupee could face downward pressure, making imports pricier for regular citizens.

impacts.target: India's forex reserves (total foreign currency savings)
impacts.rationale: Continued spending to prop up the currency eats into national reserves, reducing the country's financial buffer against global economic shocks — generally concerning for long-term stability.

impacts.target: Imported goods (like crude oil and electronics)
impacts.rationale: A softer rupee or exhausted defense tools mean India pays more rupees to buy foreign goods, driving up local inflation and hitting household budgets.
Export-heavy sectors often benefit when the rupee depreciates because their foreign earnings convert into more rupees, which can be good for shareholders.

watch_next: Future updates on India's total foreign exchange reserve numbers
Any shift in RBI statements regarding the 'market-determined' exchange rate policy
analysis.caveats: If global oil prices drop sharply or foreign investments surge unexpectedly, the pressure on the rupee could ease without requiring a major policy change.

events.headline: New trade-restrictive measures surge but WTO members step up trade facilitation efforts

items.title: New trade-restrictive measures surge but WTO members step up trade facilitation efforts
items.summary: The pace of newly-introduced tariffs and other non-facilitating measures rose sharply in the first half of 2026, while the stockpile of such measures reached a record level, according to the WTO Director-General's latest annual overview of developments in the international trading environment. At the same time, WTO members introduced a significant number of trade-facilitating measures, helping to sustain global trade flows despite heightened geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty.

events.article_text:
trade monitoring — WTO-wide reports on trade-related developments

Stockpile of other trade and trade related import and export measures introduced since 2009 and in force as of the reporting date

In 2025, WTO members and observers introduced 1,229 new trade and trade-related measures, according to the report. During the first half of 2026 alone, a further 1,048 measures were recorded, reflecting a substantially higher monthly pace of trade policy activity. The increase was broad-based across the membership and not limited to the largest trading economies. These trends were also identified by the Trade Policy Activity (TPA) Index, which WTO and IMF economists updated in July.

New trade-facilitating measures accelerated sharply in the first half of 2026. WTO members and observers introduced 466 such measures, exceeding the 391 recorded during all of 2025. In the first half of 2026, new import-facilitating measures covered an estimated USD 1.3 trillion (5.2 per cent) of world imports, while export-facilitating measures reached a record USD 570 billion (2.3 per cent) of world exports). This is more than five times the level recorded in 2025. Much of this increase reflected temporary actions adopted in response to trade disruptions associated with the Strait of Hormuz situation.

At the same time, members introduced 333 new restrictive and other non-facilitating trade measures in the first half of 2026 alone, exceeding the 300 recorded during all of 2025. Import-related measures covered USD 2.0 trillion (8.0 per cent)) of world imports in the first half of 2026, while export-related measures covered USD 794 billion (3.2 per cent) in world exports.

The report covers trade and trade-related measures up to 30 June 2026, presenting annual data for 2025 and semi-annual data for the period January to June 2026, while also tracking the accumulation of measures introduced since 2009 and still in force.

As of 30 June 2026, the stockpile(1) of import-related restrictive and other non-facilitating measures introduced since 2009 and still in force, covered USD 5.4 trillion of trade, equivalent to 21.3 per cent of world imports. The stockpile of such export-related measures reached USD 1.5 trillion, covering 6.3 per cent of world exports. Both figures represent the highest levels recorded since the WTO trade monitoring began.

Highlighting two contrasting trends, WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said: "On the one hand, import tariffs and other non-facilitating measures affect significant shares of global trade, and the stockpile of trade-restrictive measures continues to grow, reaching its highest level since WTO trade monitoring began in 2009 and affecting an increasing share of global trade. On the other hand, WTO members have stepped up their efforts to facilitate trade, introducing measures that have helped businesses navigate recent disruptions and maintain the flow of goods across borders."

"In most sectors examined, new import-facilitating measures covered a larger share of imports than new restrictive and non-facilitating measures. The only exceptions were electric vehicles and photovoltaic cells, where major economies have been heavily competing for market share, which has sparked lots of trade policy debates recently", DG Okonjo-Iweala noted.

She added: "I welcome these trade-facilitating actions and encourage WTO members to build on this positive momentum. At a time of a rapidly changing global trading environment, restraint in the use of new trade restrictions and a continued commitment to open, predictable and transparent trade will be essential for supporting economic growth, strengthening resilience and preserving the benefits of the multilateral trading system."

Global trade proved more resilient than expected in the first half of 2026 despite the disruption caused by the Middle East conflict, driven in large part by surging demand for AI-enabling goods, according to the latest "Global Trade Outlook and Statistics" released on 8 October 2026. The WTO has revised its forecast for world merchandise trade volume growth in 2026 upward to 3.9 per cent, from the 1.9 per cent baseline forecast issued in March. In value terms, merchandise trade increased by around 15 per cent year-on-year during the first half of 2026.

Commercial services trade growth is now forecast at 3.3 per cent in 2026, down from the March forecast of 4.8 per cent owing largely to the impact of the Middle East conflict on transport and travel services. Nevertheless, commercial services trade in value terms increased by around 14 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026.

Trade remedy actions continued to be widely used, although the trade affected by these measures remained limited. In 2025, WTO members initiated 391 investigations, averaging 32.6 initiations per month. During the first half of 2026, 218 new investigations were initiated, averaging 36.3 per month, while only 31 trade remedy actions were terminated. Anti-dumping measures remained the most frequently used trade remedy instrument.

WTO members and observers introduced 130 new measures affecting trade in services in 2025 and a further 52 measures during the first six months of 2026. Most were aimed at facilitating trade or strengthening regulatory frameworks, while many applied across multiple sectors and modes of supply.

WTO members and observers continued to make extensive use of general economic support measures, with industrial and agricultural support remaining at historically high levels and increasingly focused on competitiveness, resilience, security of supply and climate objectives.

The WTO reports on trade monitoring entitled "Overview of Developments in the International Trading Environment" have been published continuously since 2009, as mandated by WTO rules. Issued under the responsibility of the WTO Director-General, these reports aim to assist the Trade Policy Review Body in analyzing the impact of international trade dev

analysis.tldr: A surge in global trade barriers and easing rules means Indian exporters face shifting hurdles abroad, while global supply chains reshape around disruptions.
the_story: In 2025, WTO members introduced 1,229 new trade measures, and a further 1,048 were recorded in the first half of 2026.
New trade-facilitating measures hit 466 in the first half of 2026, driven by temporary actions responding to the Strait of Hormuz situation, covering USD 1.3 trillion of world imports.
Members introduced 333 new restrictive trade measures in the first half of 2026, with import-related restrictions covering USD 2.0 trillion of world imports.
The total stockpile of active import-related restrictions since 2009 reached a record USD 5.4 trillion, or 21.3 per cent of world imports.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala noted that electric vehicles and photovoltaic cells were exceptions where import-facilitating measures did not outpace restrictions due to heavy market competition.
analysis.what_happened: Governments across the world rushed to introduce both barriers (like tariffs) and helpful measures (like easing import rules) at a much faster monthly pace in 2025 and early 2026. The surge in helpful measures was largely a temporary response to trade disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, while long-term restrictive rules continued to pile up to their highest levels since 2009.
analysis.analogy: It is like a crowded highway where some authorities are suddenly opening up fast lanes to let traffic bypass roadblocks, while other checkpoints keep adding more toll gates and inspection queues.
why_it_matters_india: Global trade policy activity accelerates -> WTO members add hundreds of new restrictions and facilitations -> International supply chains and shipping routes face frequent rule changes

Major economies heavily restrict sectors like electric vehicles and solar panels -> Intense global competition shifts export destinations -> Indian manufacturing and green energy components face fluctuating external demand

Temporary trade-facilitating measures offset Middle East disruptions -> Global trade volume growth forecast for 2026 is revised upward to 3.9 per cent -> Shipping and demand patterns for Indian goods experience mixed signals
Accumulated global trade restrictions reach a record 21.3 per cent of world imports -> Compliance and trade friction increase -> Indian exporters navigate a more complex regulatory environment abroad

impacts.rationale: Global trade proving resilient with upwardly revised growth forecasts can lift sentiment for Indian multinational and export-oriented companies, which is generally good for market investors.
Commercial services trade growing globally despite disruptions supports tech spending, benefiting major Indian IT service providers — positive for investors holding these shares.
A massive stockpile of trade-restrictive measures covering trillions in imports can increase friction and supply costs globally, potentially pushing up everyday prices — bad for household budgets.

watch_next: Future updates from the World Trade Organization on trade-restrictive versus trade-facilitating measures
Developments in global trade policies affecting electric vehicles and solar cells
analysis.caveats: The report tracks global aggregates up to June 2026, so rapid policy reversals by major economies could alter these trade flows quickly.

events.headline: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time

items.title: Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time
items.summary: Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon… The post Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time appeared first on Carbon Brief .

events.article_text:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and COP31 co-president Australia are the largest exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in history, reveals Carbon Brief analysis.

Since 1850, the three nations – and other major fossil-fuel exporters – have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 in the form of gas, oil and coal that has been burned in other countries.

Carbon Brief’s analysis of extraction-based CO2 emissions is based on figures compiled by Robbie Andrew, a senior researcher at Norwegian climate institute CICERO.

It shows that Australia is responsible for more than twice as much global warming when including emissions from its fossil-fuel exports, while Saudi Arabia has caused more than four times as much.

Australia has been under pressure for continuing to expand its fossil-fuel production ahead of the UN climate summit in Antalya, where it is co-president with host nation Turkey.

In contrast, nations that are heavily reliant on energy imports – such as Japan or Germany – have are responsible for far lower shares of planet-warming emissions, if responsibility passes to fossil-fuel producers.

There are many different ways to assign historical responsibility for current global warming.

Carbon Brief has previously published analysis based on territorial emissions, the consumption of imported goods, according to colonial rule or based on historical emissions per capita.

This year is expected to be around 1.5C hotter than pre-industrial temperatures. Next year is forecast to be the hottest on record, at around 1.7C of warming.

This year-to-year variation is due to natural variability, such as El Niño. However, approximately 100% of global warming to date is the result of human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

The burning of fossil fuels since the industrial revolution is the largest contributor to this.

Since there is a direct link between each tonne of CO2 and each fraction of a degree of warming, historical fossil-fuel emissions can be tied to responsibility for current climate change.

This is typically calculated on the basis of historical territorial CO2 emissions, according to where in the world the fossil fuels are burned. It is also possible to assign historical responsibility on a “consumption” basis, according to where goods are used.

Historical emissions are often counted by country, but this puts the focus on populous nations. Alternatively, responsibility can be assigned per capita, based on today’s populations.

A less-familiar way to look at the question of historical responsibility is to consider where fossil fuels are extracted. This puts the spotlight on major fossil-fuel exporters.

The figure below shows that Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the largest CO2 exporters of all time, based on emissions from exported fossil fuels since 1850.

(The allocation is based on extraction taking place within current national borders. Emissions under the former USSR, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia are allocated among constituent countries, based on their share of emissions at the time of separation.)

Other major CO2 exporters, based on their overseas sales of fossil fuels since 1850, include Venezuela, Iran, Norway, the United Arab Emirates and Canada.

Between them, these major coal, oil and gas producers have exported hundreds of billions of tonnes of CO2 over the past 175 years, according to Carbon Brief’s analysis.

The analysis shows that overall, the US and China retain the largest responsibility for historical warming under extraction-based accounting, despite having been net CO2 importers since 1850.

The US has large resources of coal, oil and gas, but was nevertheless a major oil importer until after the shale revolution in the early 2000s.

China remains a major oil and gas importer, describing itself as “rich in coal, lacking oil and gas”.

Russia remains in third place, as shown in the figure below, despite gaining responsibility for an extra 69bn tonnes of CO2 from exported fossil fuels.

The UK becomes the fourth-largest historical emitter, climbing above Germany due to the latter’s reliance on fossil-fuel imports.

Saudi Arabia becomes responsible for the world’s fifth-largest share of historical warming when including its fossil-fuel exports, which increase its cumulative emissions more than fourfold.

Australia also climbs up the rankings, becoming one of the top-ten largest emitters when including its fossil-fuel exports. This more than doubles its share of historical emissions.

Nations that drop down the rankings under extraction-based accounting, due to their reliance on fossil-fuel imports, include Germany, India, France and COP31 host Turkey.

Japan is a particularly notable example, as it is almost completely reliant on fossil-fuel imports. The nation is the sixth-largest emitter on a territorial basis and the 34th-largest on an extraction basis.

When considering population sizes, major fossil-fuel exporters have the highest extraction-based CO2 emissions since 1850, as shown in the figure below.

Small nations that export large amounts of oil and gas are particularly prominent on this list, including Brunei, Kuwait, Qatar, Norway and Trinidad and Tobago.

Andrew tells Carbon Brief that while the extraction-based accounting offers an alternative perspective on historical responsibility for warming, it also raises complex questions. He explains:

“At the end of the day, it’s not solely the responsibility of extracting countries that fuels are combusted; it’s joint responsibility between extractors, producers and consumers.”

He adds that responsibility for past decisions is shared by many actors. For example, he notes that oil production in the Middle East was historically “developed by and for western powers”.

National emissions under extraction-based accounting come from a dataset developed by Robbie Andrew and covering the period from 1850-2025.

analysis.tldr: New carbon accounting methods place India lower in historical emissions rankings due to its reliance on imported energy, potentially altering global climate negotiations.
the_story: Carbon Brief analysis reveals Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia are the largest historical exporters of carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions since 1850.
The analysis calculates emissions based on where fossil fuels are extracted rather than where they are burned, using figures compiled by researcher Robbie Andrew.
When accounting for fossil-fuel exports, Australia's global warming responsibility more than doubles, and Saudi Arabia's increases more than fourfold.
Nations heavily reliant on energy imports, including India, Germany, France, and Turkey, drop down the historical emissions rankings under this extraction-based accounting.
analysis.what_happened: A new research analysis looks at historical climate responsibility by tracking where fossil fuels like coal, oil, and gas were dug up rather than where they were finally burned. Because countries like India rely heavily on importing the energy they use, this different way of counting shifts the blame for past global warming away from energy-importing nations toward major energy-exporting countries.
analysis.analogy: It is like blaming the farmer who grew and sold the tobacco rather than just the person who smoked the cigarette.
why_it_matters_india: India relies heavily on importing fossil fuels from other nations to meet its energy needs.
Under extraction-based accounting, India's historical responsibility for climate change drops in global rankings because it did not extract those fuels within its borders.
This changes how international climate talks view historical blame, potentially easing pressure on India during global negotiations.
However, shifting global pressure onto fossil-fuel exporters could eventually affect the global price and availability of imported oil, gas, and coal.

impacts.target: Crude oil import costs for India
impacts.rationale: If international climate pressure eventually restricts fossil fuel extraction in exporting nations like Saudi Arabia and Russia, tighter supply could raise import costs for India, which is bad for household budgets and inflation.

watch_next: Discussions at upcoming UN climate summits regarding how historical emissions and responsibility are measured
Changes in fossil-fuel production and export policies in major exporting nations like Australia, Russia, and Saudi Arabia
analysis.caveats: This new accounting method is an analytical perspective and does not immediately change current international climate laws or financial agreements.

events.headline: RIP to the $1.45 Trillion FY2027 Defense Budget

items.title: RIP to the $1.45 Trillion FY2027 Defense Budget
items.summary: The 2026 Congressional midterms appear to have dealt a final death blow to the Trump administration’s prospective $1.45 trillion Fiscal Year 2027 Department of Defense budget request. While there remains a path forward to salvage the base budget request of $1.1 trillion, it is exceedingly difficult to envision a legislative pathway for the $350 billion reconciliation request. The reconciliation request has always faced considerable obstacles stemming from divisions within the Congressional Republican caucus, but the extent of the midterm defeat and limited legislative calendar make its prospec

events.article_text:
Once this has been accepted, there remains considerable uncertainty about what’s next. Looking at the defense budget and defense spending, there are four pressing questions: Whether Congress can agree on FY2027 appropriations; what can be moved from the reconciliation request into the base budget (and, relatedly, what is cut to accommodate it); whether there will be supplemental funding (either as a standalone bill or as part of a funding deal) to refill accounts drawn down by operations in Iran; and whether yet another continuing resolution will be passed kicking the can on funding until the 120th Congress can be seated.

This backlog will create obstacles to the Pentagon moving forward as quickly as it would like on its stated priorities and reassert the supremacy of Congress in the budgeting process.

Defense spending has been in a period of rapid growth. Between base appropriations and the One Big Beautiful Bill passed in 2025, the Department of Defense expects FY2026 defense spending to exceed $1 trillion. This April, the FY2027 request came out even higher: Base spending would be $1.1 trillion, while an additional $350 billion was requested in another reconciliation bill. Defense spending would grow by almost 44 percent over the FY2026 level. A new age of defense spending was coming.

However, as my earlier writing for War on the Rocks made clear, Congress is the entity ultimately responsible for spending decisions, and the odds of passage for this sort of increase were always somewhat long. Congressional Republicans may be more favorable to increased defense spending, but they also count amongst their number a significant number of deficit hawks. As the price of their support for such an increase, deficit hawks would have demanded cuts to non-defense spending (either discretionary spending or mandatory spending such as Medicaid or Medicare) that more moderate Republicans would have opposed. The 2025 reconciliation bill finessed this through large tax cuts —something the entire caucus agrees upon — with increased defense and border security spending alongside significant cuts to discretionary and mandatory spending in areas the moderates accepted.

In an election year, when members are reluctant to take potentially controversial votes, an even larger defense increase ($350 billion, compared to last year’s $151 billion) was going to be a difficult lift. Even traditional defense hawks like former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell had concerns about going through reconciliation for such a significant percentage of the defense budget. This is because reconciliation money, existing outside the normal appropriations process, is much harder for Congress to control and direct. Balking at the full reconciliation request, the House did begin the process for a smaller reconciliation package focused on funding combat operations in Iran, but it’s comprised of different funding than what was found in the FY2027 reconciliation request, and only has space for $60 billion in defense spending. It remains the only live vehicle for a potential lame duck push.

Now, after the 2026 midterms, the already challenging legislative math is complicated by two additional factors: the limits of the legislative calendar, and maintaining the focus of members who have been swept out of office. The already fine margins in the House (2 vote margin) and Senate (3 vote margin) during the 119th Congress will be sorely tested as members who have lost are swept out of their offices and begin to envision post-Congressional life.

The lame duck calendar is short, with only five scheduled legislative work weeks before the end of the 119th Congress. In that time, Congress will need to work through a range of must-pass and pending legislation including the National Defense Authorization Act, the farm bill, Iran operations funding, lapsed Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act authorization, permitting reform, college sports reform, various other expiring authorizations (Export-Import Bank, highway funding), and the main one, the end of the current continuing resolution on Dec. 11. Failure to pass the last one would result in a government shutdown. The administration can push hard for a reconciliation bill, but it will be competing with these other issues for floor time.

Passing a full reconciliation bill takes time. First, both the House and Senate would need to agree to a budget resolution. In the Senate, that requires a potentially grueling “vote-a-rama” on a range of Democratic amendments. Then, the committees identified in the resolution must prepare and pass their pieces of legislation. Matching legislation must then pass both the House and the Senate. While none of this is subject to the filibuster, it will require Republicans in both chambers to stick together throughout. Given their narrow margins, the calendar would normally be the primary concern, but after the midterm results, there will almost certainly be attendance issues.

The full results of the 2026 midterm elections are still pending, but the high-level results are clear: Democrats will have picked up between eight and nine Senate seats and have flipped at least 40 House seats. These numbers also undersell the turnover. In the Senate, between 13 and 15 members will be departing when you include retirements and primary losses. In the House that number will almost certainly exceed 50, and may well rise above 60 departing Republican members.

It can’t be emphasized enough that members who have lost or are leaving office are going to be more difficult to whip in support of a bill. While Senators are given the decency of keeping their offices until January, this author knows from personal experience that the House of Representatives will typically kick members out of their offices by Dec. 1. Members who are looking for work or trying to decide what to do next will not want to hang around for something they may not feel passionately about. This is doubly so f

analysis.tldr: Political gridlock in the US over a massive defense budget cut could ripple into global market sentiment, shifting foreign investments that affect Indian stocks.
the_story: The US Department of Defense expected FY2026 spending to exceed $1 trillion, and the FY2027 request aimed for $1.1 trillion in base spending plus an additional $350 billion via a reconciliation bill.
The odds of passing this 44 percent jump were slim because Congressional deficit hawks demanded cuts to other non-defense spending that moderate Republicans opposed.

The 2026 midterms resulted in major political shifts, with Democrats picking up 8-9 Senate seats and flipping at least 40 House seats, leaving a short legislative calendar and departing members hard to rally.
analysis.what_happened: The proposed massive $1.45 trillion US defense budget for fiscal year 2027 is effectively dead due to fierce political division, upcoming leadership and member changes after the 2026 midterms, and a severely restricted calendar. Lawmakers cannot agree on how to fund the increase without cutting other vital programs, and departing politicians have little appetite to pass complicated fiscal packages.
analysis.analogy: It is like a corporate board of directors fighting over a massive expansion plan while half the board members have just been fired and refuse to show up for work.
why_it_matters_india: US political deadlock creates uncertainty in global financial markets.
Global investors adjust their risk appetite when major US spending plans collapse.
Shifts in global risk appetite can cause foreign institutional investors (big international investment funds) to alter their capital allocations.
This movement of foreign capital directly impacts the valuation of Indian equities and the stability of the rupee.

impacts.rationale: Global market jitters from US budget gridlock can cause foreign investors to pull back risk, which typically weighs on Indian stocks — generally bad for local investors.
Uncertainty in US fiscal policy can strengthen the dollar index, causing the rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars), making imports costlier for India.

watch_next: Whether the US Congress passes a continuing resolution to avoid a government shutdown by December 11
Updates on smaller standalone defense funding bills like the $60 billion combat operations package
analysis.caveats: The text cuts off mid-sentence at the end, but the core analysis regarding the impossibility of passing the FY2027 defense budget under current political math remains clear.

events.headline: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance

items.title: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance
items.summary: This photograph taken on September 6, 2026 shows a placard opposing data centers displayed on a water dispenser during the People's Convention on AI Data Centers event at Visakhapatnam in India's Andhra Pradesh state. Construction of a massive Google data centre in the Indian city of Visakhapatnam, often called Vizag, has been met with resistance from residents, who fear the impact on the environment and their lives. But the tech giant says its "gigawatt-scale" AI facility -- in southern Andhra Pradesh state, part of a $15 billion investment -- will use air cooling systems, and not water from

events.article_text:
After ChatGPT was released in November 2022, the tech industry was quick to herald the chatbot as the marker of a new wave of technological progress. As companies pushed to create more powerful AI models, the water demand of their ambitions took a while to become clear. In April 2023, a research paper out of the University of California estimated that training the large language model behind the initial version of ChatGPT had required 185,000 gallons of water. For every extended conversation someone had with the chatbot or every time they asked it to write an email, they were effectively pouring a bottle of water down the drain.

That statistic got a lot of play when it was released. It became an early warning sign of what was coming as companies pushed chatbots as a universal technology that could replace psychologists, educators, lawyers, and even people’s friends or partners.

As public concern grew, Google and OpenAI came out with their own figures. The companies suggested that querying one of their chatbots used mere drops of water. Independent researchers were not impressed, arguing the companies were taking a narrow view of the water use necessary to power and cool increasingly monstrous data centers. Those water demands can be quite significant too.

A hyperscale data center can suck up between 1 and 5 million gallons of water a day, comparable to the amount used by a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people — depending on the part of the world we’re talking about. Consider how these companies often cluster data centers together and it becomes obvious what a challenge it can be to supply them.

The water demands of individual data centers are also continuing to grow. It’s not just that they need more water for cooling as they become larger and contain more servers. The graphics processing units (GPUs) that power generative AI are much more resource-intensive than the chips and storage devices that traditionally filled data center racks. GPUs run harder and throw off more heat, meaning they also need more energy or water to keep them cool.

Data centers cannot just use any kind of water either; it has to be clean enough to ensure the equipment and pipes are not damaged. Tapping into public drinking water is both easier and cheaper than paying the cost of treatment themselves. That means data centers end up competing with communities over their potable water supply.

If we want to look at a part of the world where the issue of data center water use has taken center stage, there are few better countries to turn to than Chile. In October 2019, mass social demonstrations broke out across the country. One of the movement’s driving slogans was about water. It was poor timing for Google as it was fighting for approval and public support of its latest data center project, a $200 million data center project in Cerrillos, on the southwest side of Santiago.

The company made a pitch similar to the one residents in communities the world over have heard whenever a data center is proposed: that the facility would bring jobs and prosperity, and give the area a leg up on further tech investments. The reality was not so straightforward. Google’s new data center would bring a lot of short-term construction jobs but not much long-term employment. And it would need a lot of water — something Cerrillos did not have much of to spare.

Local residents were not as passive as the company had hoped. A group of concerned citizens established an organization called MOSACAT, which stands for Community Socio-Environmental Movement for Water and Land, and started poring over whatever information they could get their hands on to try to understand what the project would mean for them. “Usually these reports use quite technical language, and this is a working- class community where not many people are lawyers, for example, or experts on ecology,” explains Sebastián Lehuedé, a researcher at King’s College London who is from Chile and spent time in Cerrillos.

According to its own projections, the data center Google wanted to build in Cerrillos was poised to use 169 liters of water every single second. In just one day, the data center would consume as much water as all 80,000 residents of Cerrillos use for drinking in a year. To make matters worse, it wanted to draw that water from an underground aquifer that had been under a decree that restricted how much water could be removed since 2005. Just weeks before the project was rubber-stamped by the environmental authority, that decree had been upgraded to a complete prohibition on new extraction.

The water use estimates set off alarm bells for the residents. Chile had already been in an unprecedented drought since 2010. By 2021, more than half the country’s 19 million residents lived in areas experiencing severe water scarcity, forcing hundreds of rural communities to rely on tankers to deliver drinking water.

The local activists ultimately built the case against one of the largest companies on the planet. After months of meetings and advocacy to spread awareness, they were able to put a referendum question to the residents of Cerrillos about the project in December 2019. The results were damning: 49% of voters chose to reject the project, while 38% wanted it to go forward.

After both the municipality and community members filed claims against Google in 2020, the company returned with a new proposal in February 2022. It offered to cool the data center exclusively with air-conditioning rather than with water.

Across the city in Quilicura, opposition was building too. Microsoft announced its intention to build a data center in the community in 2022, the same year strict water-rationing rules had come into effect in Santiago. As in Cerrillos, residents were worried that another large data center would threaten their access to water and provide little in return.

Vicente Bardales, a member of the Quilicura Socio Environmental Resistance group, told Rest of World that the compa

analysis.tldr: Big tech's massive water consumption for AI could trigger tighter global regulations and higher costs, potentially influencing how data centers are built and powered in developing markets like India.
the_story: A University of California study in April 2023 estimated training the early ChatGPT model took 185,000 gallons of water, with every extended chat using about a bottle's worth.

A hyperscale data center consumes between 1 million and 5 million gallons of water daily, rivalling a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people due to the heavy cooling needs of generative AI graphics processing units (GPUs).
Data centers require clean water to prevent pipe and equipment damage, often opting to use public drinking water which creates direct competition with local communities.

In Cerrillos, Chile, local residents formed a group called MOSACAT and successfully pushed back against a $200 million Google data center that was projected to use 169 liters of water per second from a restricted aquifer during a severe drought.

Faced with community pushback and legal challenges, Google updated its proposal in February 2022 to cool the Cerrillos facility using air-conditioning instead of water, while Microsoft faced similar resistance in Quilicura.
analysis.what_happened: Artificial intelligence tools and data centers require enormous amounts of electricity and clean water for cooling. As tech giants built more facilities in water-scarce regions like Santiago, Chile, local communities organized resistance movements over competition for drinking water.
analysis.analogy: It is like a massive factory moving into a small village, using up all the water from the local well, and leaving the villagers with dry taps while promising jobs that mostly vanish after construction ends.
why_it_matters_india: Global tech companies face rising public scrutiny and regulatory hurdles over their resource usage.
As countries tighten environmental rules for data centers, building and running these facilities could become costlier worldwide.
Higher operational costs for global tech giants can ripple into higher prices for cloud computing services used by businesses everywhere, including India.
India itself faces severe water stress in many urban centers, making local data center expansions sensitive to similar resource-competition concerns.

impacts.rationale: Stricter environmental rules and redesigning data centers to use less water or alternative cooling will increase expenses for tech firms, which can be neutral to negative for tech stock margins.

impacts.target: Cloud computing and software service costs for businesses
impacts.rationale: If cooling and compliance expenses rise for data center operators, those costs may trickle down to corporate users of cloud infrastructure, mildly increasing software expenses.

watch_next: New environmental regulations or zoning rules for data centers in developing nations
Technological shifts by major tech companies toward air-cooling or closed-loop water recycling systems
analysis.caveats: The original article cuts off near the end, but the core reporting on water conflicts in Chile and data center consumption remains clear.

items.title: PSBs integrate ESG parameters into companies' credit risk assessment

the_story: Public sector banks (state-run banks) are incorporating ESG parameters (environment, social, and governance rules) into their credit risk assessment (evaluation of whether a borrower can repay a loan).
Seven banks, led by the State Bank of India (India's largest government-owned bank), are spearheading this change to improve how they approve loans.
These lenders are creating climate risk frameworks (systems to check weather and climate dangers) for loan approvals and using standard methods to calculate greenhouse gas emissions.
The EASE 9.0 Reform Agenda (a government program to update and improve state-run banks) is keeping track of these changes.
analysis.what_happened: Government-owned banks are changing how they decide to give out loans by adding environmental and social checks. Driven by the EASE 9.0 Reform Agenda modernization plan, banks like the State Bank of India are building new rules to check climate risks and track company pollution levels before handing out money.
analysis.analogy: It is like a strict fitness coach checking not just your gym membership, but your daily diet and sleep habits before letting you join the elite team.
why_it_matters_india: Banks adopt new climate risk and emission tracking rules ->
Companies that pollute heavily or ignore worker safety face stricter background checks ->
Green-friendly businesses find it easier to borrow, while heavy polluters may see higher borrowing costs ->
Overall lending standards improve, protecting the banking system from bad loans tied to environmental disasters.

impacts.target: Cost of borrowing for heavy polluting industries
impacts.rationale: Stricter ESG checks mean polluting companies may face tougher terms or higher interest rates to borrow from state banks — bad for those businesses, but good for pushing cleaner practices.

impacts.target: State-owned bank loan portfolios (quality of loans)
impacts.rationale: By filtering out climate and social risks early, banks reduce bad loans, which is good for the stability of India's banking system.

history.title: A budget that broke the pension system in three days
history.what: A new British government announced large unfunded tax cuts. Within three days UK government bond yields spiked so violently that pension funds faced collapse, and the Bank of England had to step in with emergency bond buying. The Prime Minister resigned within seven weeks.
history.why: Pension funds had used a strategy called liability-driven investing, which borrows against bonds to match long-term obligations. It works while yields move gradually. When yields jumped, the funds faced collateral calls, and the only way to meet them was to sell the very bonds that were falling — pushing yields higher still. Hidden leverage almost nobody outside the industry had noticed.
history.impact: The pound hit an all-time low against the dollar. Mortgage rates jumped and hundreds of mortgage products were pulled within days. The government's entire fiscal plan was reversed.
history.policy: The Bank of England bought long-dated bonds for a strictly limited window to break the loop, then regulators forced pension funds to hold far larger liquidity buffers against exactly this scenario.
history.consequence: It established that a rich, stable country with its own currency can still be disciplined by the bond market within days. Finance ministers everywhere became noticeably more careful about announcing unfunded spending.
history.pattern: The dangerous leverage is the leverage nobody discusses, usually because it sits inside an institution everyone considers boring. Ask who is forced to sell when prices fall — forced sellers turn a move into a spiral.
history.india_echo: India's fiscal deficit and government borrowing programme are worth watching for this reason. A bond market's patience is not infinite, and when it runs out it runs out in days rather than quarters.
history.watch_for: Bond yields rising while the currency falls. Normally higher yields support a currency; when both move the wrong way together, the market is questioning the government's credibility rather than its interest rates.
